articles.title: RBI hikes repo rate to 5.5%, first increase since February 2023, shifts stance to 'calibrated tightening'
articles.summary: The RBI raised its repo rate 25 basis points to 5.5%, its first hike since February 2023, and changed its policy stance to signal that only a hike or a pause is on the table next. It also raised its FY27 growth forecast to 7.1%.
articles.body:
The Reserve Bank of India raised its benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% on Wednesday, its first increase since February 2023, joining the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan in a global tightening move this month. The Monetary Policy Committee also changed its policy stance from 'neutral' to 'calibrated tightening', with four of its six members voting for the shift. At the same time, the MPC raised its FY27 growth forecast by 40 basis points to 7.1%, matching the latest upgraded World Bank assessment released the day before.

Governor Sanjay Malhotra explained the stance change directly: "given current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term, and policy action can only be a hike or a pause, depending on evolving conditions." The MPC's own statement said inflation and its outlook "are not benign as they were last year," and Malhotra called recalibrating the policy rate "imperative." This is the first rate increase since Malhotra took charge in December 2024, a tenure that until now had delivered 125 basis points of cuts and a 100-basis-point cut in the cash reserve ratio.

Markets reacted immediately. The benchmark 10-year bond yield climbed to 7.24%, a near three-year high, up 5 basis points on the day. The rupee slipped to 96.84 per dollar, close to its record low of 96.96 hit on May 20. Malhotra, responding to a question, said the rupee may be undervalued and described short-term financial-market moves as "irrational."

The global backdrop matters here. The Fed and the ECB each raised rates 25 basis points in mid-September, and Japan followed two days later, raising rates to tame yields that had scaled levels last seen in 1996. With borrowing costs rising from Tokyo to Washington, the RBI faced a widening gap it could not ignore, on top of its own domestic problem: an energy supply chokehold from the West Asia conflict and scanty rains, which together pushed the RBI to raise its FY27 inflation projection by 20 basis points.

Analysts are split on how far this goes. Nomura read the stance change as an "overly hawkish start," calling it pre-emptive signalling rather than a commitment, and still expects one more 25-basis-point hike in December followed by a pause. SBI's chief economist, Soumya Kanti Ghosh, puts real odds on a 50-basis-point hike in December given the inflation trajectory. Jefferies has gone further, raising its total estimate for this hiking cycle to 75-100 basis points, up from 50 earlier.

For a trader or a borrower, the direct read-through is straightforward: EMIs on floating-rate loans will rise, rate-sensitive sectors such as autos, real estate and NBFCs face higher funding costs, and bond yields are likely to stay elevated until the inflation data clearly turns. The next test is the December MPC meeting, and before that, Monday's CPI print for September.

categories: Economy & Banking bodies (RBI, SEBI, NABARD, IBRD, IMF, etc.)

facts.fact: RBI repo rate raised to 5.5% on 2026-10-07/08, first hike since February 2023

articles.title: Houthi missile attack on Riyadh airport sets off a wave of Gulf flight suspensions
articles.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that set a Saudia aircraft on fire. Air India, IndiGo and Lufthansa have all suspended Riyadh flights as the conflict escalates.
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed a missile attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, with reports that a Saudia Airlines aircraft caught fire after being damaged. The attack has triggered an immediate response from international carriers. Lufthansa and Air India suspended their Riyadh flights, and the Indian Express separately confirmed that IndiGo also suspended flights to the Saudi capital after the attack.

The disruption is not confined to Riyadh. The Indian Embassy in Riyadh has issued an advisory to Indian nationals, and Air India, IndiGo and Akasa Air have all taken precautionary steps around Saudi airspace and airports, according to reports from the same period. This is the clearest sign yet that the Saudi-Houthi conflict, which has simmered through the West Asia war, is now directly disrupting commercial aviation at a major Gulf hub rather than just regional shipping and oil infrastructure.

The timing connects to several other threads in this edition. Oil prices have been volatile through the week on exactly this kind of escalation risk, with reports noting markets tumbling to an 18-month low as US-Iran tensions lifted crude, before easing again on Friday as indications emerged that US military action against Iran is unlikely before the November midterm elections. Riyadh's airport is not a minor node: it is one of the busiest hubs in the Gulf, and any sustained disruption there affects connections for Indian travellers and cargo moving through Saudi Arabia.

For Indian carriers, the decision to suspend Riyadh flights is a safety-first call that will have schedule and revenue consequences, particularly for routes that connect Indian cities to Europe and North America via Gulf hubs. It also sits alongside a separate, specifically maritime risk this week: Indian seafarers transiting the Strait of Hormuz have faced attacks on commercial shipping, and the government has confirmed that crew remain stranded in the strait. Together, the airport attack and the shipping incidents point to a West Asia conflict that is now touching Indian transport links on both sea and air.

What to watch: whether other carriers follow Lufthansa, Air India and IndiGo in suspending Riyadh routes, how long the suspension lasts, and whether Saudi authorities disclose the extent of damage at King Khalid International Airport. Any escalation beyond this one attack would widen the disruption further.

articles.title: 139 Indian crew stranded in Strait of Hormuz as shipping ministry tracks seafarers in real time
articles.summary: An official briefing said Indian crew remain stranded across ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, after recent attacks on commercial vessels in the region. The shipping ministry says it is tracking every Indian seafarer in the area in real time.
articles.body:
An official briefing this week confirmed that Indian seafarers remain stranded on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, as the West Asia war continues to put commercial shipping at risk. The headline figure attributed to the briefing, as reported, named both a cumulative toll since the war began and a count of crew currently stuck in the strait; the portion of the briefing available for this edition describes specific recent incidents rather than a single confirmed death count, so that overall toll should be treated as an official claim pending fuller confirmation, not an independently verified figure.

What is clearer from the briefing is the pattern of recent incidents. Eleven Indian crew members were injured when a projectile struck a Panama-flagged vessel while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The Ministry of External Affairs condemned the attack and expressed "deep concern" over the "targeting of commercial shipping," calling for dialogue and diplomacy to end the conflict. In a separate incident in the Black Sea, a Russian drone strike caused a fire on a Turkish-owned civilian cargo vessel, killing at least two foreign crew and injuring others, including an Indian national.

The shipping ministry says it has built a real-time tracking system for every seafarer working in these high-risk areas, covering vessel position, crew strength, crew welfare, threat assessment, intended voyage and the availability of food, fuel and medicines. As of the briefing, two Indian-flagged ships and six India-bound ships were in the Strait of Hormuz.

The briefing also gave context on why this matters at scale. India has gone from the world's fifth-largest to its second-largest supplier of seafarers in twelve years, with its seafarer workforce growing from 1.27 lakh to 3.23 lakh and now accounting for more than 12% of the global total. Active women seafarers rose from 1,599 in 2021 to 7,033 in 2025, supported by the Sagar Mein Samman initiative, and the government has set a target, called Mission 20%, to raise India's share of the global seafarer workforce by 2030.

Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal used the briefing to note rising foreign orders for Indian-built ships and said countries including Belgium have expressed willingness to collaborate on green shipping. He also held bilateral talks with Saudi Arabia, Belgium and Bhutan covering port investment, green shipping corridors and using the Brahmaputra as a trade gateway for Bhutan.

For India's maritime and logistics sectors, and for families of seafarers currently at sea near a live conflict zone, the practical question is whether the Strait of Hormuz route stays navigable. Watch for further MEA statements and whether insurers or shipping lines reroute away from the strait.

articles.title: Sensex rebounds 879 points, Nifty IT leads as crude eases and geopolitical fears cool
articles.summary: The Sensex and Nifty snapped a two-day decline on Friday, helped by IT stocks and easing oil prices. Analysts say the rally depends on whether Q2 earnings hold up and FII selling eases.
articles.body:
The Sensex and the Nifty 50 rebounded from a two-day losing streak on Friday, helped by broad-based buying, advancing IT shares and falling oil prices. The Sensex rose 879.09 points, or 1.23%, to close at 72,472.33, and the Nifty 50 added 288.65 points, or 1.3%, to 22,520.45. In the closing auction session, the gains extended further: the Sensex rose 951.42 points, or 1.33%, to 72,544.66, and the Nifty finished at 22,535.65, up 303.85 points or 1.37%.

The rally was broad. The Nifty Midcap 100 rose 1.56% and the Nifty Smallcap 100 rose 0.54%. Sector-wise, Nifty IT was the standout gainer, while Nifty Oil and Gas was the worst performer. Apollo Hospitals Enterprise, ITC and Eicher Motors led gains on the Nifty 50.

Geojit Investments' head of research, Vinod Nair, attributed the move to a relief rally built on value buying and short covering after the recent sharp correction. IT stocks led the recovery on the back of a strong start to the Q2 earnings season and growing confidence in AI-driven revenue opportunities, a reference to results like TCS's, released the same week. Sentiment was also helped by easing geopolitical concerns, after indications that any US military action against Iran is unlikely before the November midterm elections, which allowed crude prices to moderate.

The rebound came with caveats attached. Persistent FII outflows and elevated global bond yields continued to temper the recovery outlook, according to the same commentary. Investors are now watching Monday's domestic CPI data for signals on the interest-rate path, following the RBI's shift to a "calibrated tightening" stance earlier in the week. Nair's view is that the sustainability of this rebound depends on whether the actual Q2 earnings season, expected to be good on a year-on-year basis, delivers.

Reading this alongside the RBI's rate decision and the previous session's sharp fall, the pattern is one of a market whipsawing between a hawkish domestic rate signal and incremental relief on the geopolitical and oil side. For a trader, Friday's rebound is best read as a bounce from oversold levels rather than a trend reversal, pending confirmation from CPI data and the broader Q2 results calendar over the following weeks.

articles.title: Sensex falls over 1,000 points after RBI's hawkish stance shift catches markets off guard
articles.summary: Benchmark indices fell sharply on Thursday as the RBI's shift to a 'calibrated tightening' stance surprised investors more than the rate hike itself. Metals, realty and oil and gas stocks were the worst hit.
articles.body:
Indian equity benchmarks fell sharply on Thursday, with the Sensex cracking over 1,000 points and the Nifty down 371 points, in what one strategist called a "market mayhem" session. "The stance has become hawkish, and the change in stance was definitely a surprise. The market is expected to remain weak, unless there is some positive surprise from Q2 earnings," said Kranthi Bathini, equity strategist at WealthMills Securities. All sectoral and broader market indices closed in the red, with metals, real estate, and oil and gas among the worst hit, because these capital-intensive sectors are the most exposed to rising interest rates.

The rupee ended the day broadly flat at 96.78 against the dollar, a day after it had fallen 0.4% to 96.77 following the RBI's policy decision, its lowest level since mid-May and within sight of its all-time low of 96.96.

What actually spooked the market was not the rate move itself. A 25-basis-point hike was widely expected. What surprised participants was the RBI's change in policy stance to "calibrated tightening." Governor Sanjay Malhotra tried to soften the reading, calling it a "milder form of tightening," but it fuelled speculation that the hiking cycle could run deeper than initially expected. The official communication, however, maintained that it is too early to pre-empt the depth of the cycle and that future action depends on incoming data.

Nomura's note captured the tension: "Despite the significance of the policy stance being changed... it seems the MPC has also tried hard to dilute its messaging and signal data dependence." The brokerage still expects one more 25-basis-point hike in December followed by a pause, calling the current move "an overly hawkish start to the hiking cycle" meant as pre-emptive signalling. Not everyone agrees that it stops there. SBI's chief economist, Soumya Kanti Ghosh, sees a real chance of a 50-basis-point hike at the December MPC meeting, citing a steepening inflation trajectory and volatile global conditions. Jefferies has gone further still, raising its total rate-hike estimate for the cycle to 75-100 basis points, up from an earlier call of 50.

Systematix Institutional Equities framed the risk for equities starkly: inflation is a "bigger challenge than the RBI acknowledges," and markets now face a double squeeze, with valuations compressing under higher rates even as earnings face pressure from rising costs and interest outgo. The backdrop makes the RBI's path hard to call: high crude oil prices from the West Asia conflict, a developing El Nino, and rising inflation are all pulling in the same direction.

TCS kicked off the Q2 earnings season the same week, which markets are now watching closely as the first real test of whether corporate results can offset the rate shock.

articles.title: TCS profit rises 15% as cost cuts offset cautious clients, AI threat to outsourcing model
articles.summary: TCS reported a 15% rise in quarterly profit to Rs 13,884 crore, beating estimates, helped by cost cuts and a weaker rupee. The company highlighted $3.1 billion in annualised AI revenue even as AI tools threaten its traditional coding-services business.
articles.body:
Tata Consultancy Services reported quarterly profit ahead of analyst estimates, helped by cost-cutting and a gradually improving contract flow at Asia's largest IT services provider. Net profit rose 15% to Rs 13,884 crore ($1.4 billion) in the three months through September, against an average analyst estimate of Rs 13,786 crore. Revenue climbed 11% to Rs 73,188 crore, aided by a weaker rupee against the dollar and the euro.

The results came with a clear tension built in. TCS's major customers in the US and Europe remain cautious on large IT projects, weighed down by geopolitical tensions and elevated inflation. At the same time, AI tools from OpenAI and Anthropic are beginning to reshape how clients procure software services, which threatens the traditional outsourcing model that TCS and peers such as Infosys built their business on: hiring large numbers of graduates to write code for clients such as Apple, Boeing and Bank of America. Investors remain sceptical of TCS's ability to navigate that shift, with the stock having lost half its value over the past two years despite the company's own AI push. TCS has also run a large cost-cutting drive alongside this quarter's results.

Tata Group chairman N Chandrasekaran predicted in June that AI agents could eventually make up half of the company's workforce, while adding that AI would also open fresh opportunities. This quarter gives some evidence for that second half of the claim: TCS said its annualised AI revenue reached $3.1 billion. Two recent deals illustrate the shift. Earlier this month, TCS agreed to bring Best Buy's India global capability centre into the fold as an AI-native unit. In August, TCS signed a Euro 1.25 billion ($1.4 billion) deal with Porsche AG to deploy AI, while also agreeing to buy Porsche's consulting unit.

Chief executive Krithi Krithivasan described the Porsche and Best Buy agreements as "a new category of transformation partnerships," saying TCS and its clients are "building repeatable value platforms that will industrialise AI at scale." TCS has also partnered with OpenAI to build AI data centres and is in similar discussions with other large technology companies. India is expected to need about 10 gigawatts of AI data-centre capacity over the next four years, much of it yet to be built, and TCS wants a share of that build-out.

India's $280 billion software services sector, which TCS leads, began by offering cheap back-office work to large international companies. It now competes directly with global technology-services firms such as Accenture and IBM for cloud, automation and AI contracts with clients including Citigroup and PepsiCo. This quarter's results are a data point in a larger argument: whether Indian IT's scale and cost advantage can be redeployed fast enough to meet AI-native demand before AI itself erodes the old billing model.

articles.title: Hexaware shares jump 12% on multi-year Anthropic partnership, extending a five-session rally
articles.summary: Hexaware Technologies shares rose as much as 12% after the company signed a multi-year partnership making it a Preferred Partner in Anthropic's Claude network. The stock has gained 17% over five straight sessions.
articles.body:
Hexaware Technologies shares zoomed as much as 12% in early trade on Friday after the company announced a multi-year partnership with Anthropic. The stock opened about 4% higher at Rs 533 on the NSE and touched an intraday high of Rs 574.50. By 9:45am the stock was trading 11% higher at Rs 569, having extended its winning streak to a fifth consecutive session for a cumulative gain of 17% over that period. It was the second most active stock on the NSE by value, with 12 million shares changing hands worth Rs 671.58 crore, according to NSE data.

The deal, disclosed in an exchange filing, makes Hexaware a Preferred Partner in Anthropic's Claude Partner Network. The partnership brings Claude into two of Hexaware's platforms: Zerovity, its AI-native engineering platform, and AgentVerse, its agent build-and-governance platform, which has more than 600 pre-built agents. Hexaware said it will use Claude to deliver outcome-based services across IT operations and software engineering, as enterprise clients increasingly pay for results rather than effort. The company has more than 1,100 Claude-certified professionals, and the filing said Hexaware and Anthropic will work together on go-to-market activity, joint solution development and customer deployments, with Claude training expanded across Hexaware's delivery teams.

This builds on an existing relationship: Hexaware was already authorised to resell Claude through Amazon Bedrock. The new, deeper tie-up is the kind of AI-partnership story that is becoming a differentiator for mid-sized IT services firms trying to stand out against larger rivals.

SBI Securities' head of technical and derivatives research, Sudeep Shah, described the stock as having staged a sharp rebound and now trading above its key moving averages, with the RSI showing a pickup in bullish momentum and the ADX's directional indicators suggesting buyers are gaining control. He placed immediate resistance at the Rs 590-600 zone, saying a decisive and sustained breakout above Rs 600 could extend the current move, while the Rs 520-515 zone should act as immediate support on the downside.

For an investor tracking the AI-partnership theme in Indian IT, Hexaware's move is a smaller-cap echo of the larger TCS and Infosys deals with AI labs reported this week, suggesting the AI-partnership rally is broadening beyond the largest IT names into the mid-cap services space.

articles.title: US suspends Microsoft, TCS, Infosys, Wipro and other IT firms from PERM green-card programme
articles.summary: The Trump administration suspended Microsoft and major Indian IT firms from the PERM permanent labor certification programme, accusing them of replacing American workers with cheaper foreign labour. PERM is a green-card step, separate from the H-1B visa.
articles.body:
The Trump administration has suspended Microsoft and several major technology and IT services companies, including Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant, Adobe and Capgemini, from a US programme that is a key step toward permanent residency for skilled foreign workers. The programme, Permanent Labor Certification or PERM, is administered by the US Department of Labor, which will not accept new applications or process pending ones involving the named firms. Vice President JD Vance announced the move on Thursday, accusing the companies of using foreign-worker programmes at the expense of American employees. The action is part of a broader administration crackdown on skilled-labour and immigration programmes.

It is worth being precise about what PERM actually is, because the distinction matters for how disruptive this is. PERM is a labor-certification step in the employment-based green-card process, not a green card itself and not a work visa. An employer identifies a permanent, full-time role, establishes its requirements, obtains a prevailing-wage determination, recruits for the role, and then files a PERM application asking the Department of Labor to certify that no qualified American worker is available for it. That is different from an H-1B visa, which grants temporary work status. PERM was introduced in 2005, replacing an older paper-based system called Alien Employment Certification, specifically to make the certification process more efficient.

The administration's justification is that the named companies used foreign-worker programmes to replace or undercut American workers. The named firms have not had a chance, in the reporting available, to respond in detail, but the suspension directly blocks a pathway that Indian IT companies use to move long-serving Indian employees in the US from temporary status toward permanent residency.

Markets responded in an unexpected way. A separate ET Markets report the same day noted that IT stocks largely shrugged off the PERM suspension, gaining roughly Rs 70,000 crore in a single day, which suggests investors read the suspension as a headline risk rather than a fundamental threat to near-term earnings, since PERM affects long-run green-card pipelines rather than current billable headcount.

For Indian professionals working in the US on H-1B status, and for HR teams at the affected companies, the suspension is a real complication to long-term planning even if it does not immediately affect current employment. Watch for whether the companies challenge the suspension, whether other IT services firms are added to the list, and whether the administration clarifies a timeline or conditions for restoring PERM access.

articles.title: Jewar airport to be renamed Narendra Modi International Airport, UP Cabinet decides
articles.summary: Uttar Pradesh's Cabinet approved renaming the upcoming Noida International Airport at Jewar after Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath called it a major gift to the state and said it will become UP's largest airport.
articles.body:
The upcoming Noida International Airport at Jewar in Uttar Pradesh is set to be renamed Narendra Modi International Airport, Noida-Jewar, after the state Cabinet approved the proposal on Friday. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath announced the decision after a Cabinet meeting, describing the airport as a major gift to Uttar Pradesh from the prime minister. "The Council of Ministers of Uttar Pradesh expresses its gratitude to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for gifting the state the Noida International Airport at Jewar," Adityanath said, adding that the Cabinet had approved naming it Narendra Modi International Airport, Noida-Jewar.

Adityanath said the airport is set to become Uttar Pradesh's largest, and eventually the country's largest aviation hub. The renaming proposal was announced alongside a separate Cabinet resolution honouring Modi for completing 25 years of continuous public service as a head of government, between his time as Gujarat chief minister and as prime minister. Adityanath described October 7 as a "glorious chapter" marking that 25-year milestone, and framed the renaming as part of a wider set of tributes rather than a standalone aviation decision.

For India's aviation sector, the substance to track is the airport project itself rather than its name. Jewar, once operational, is planned to be a major new gateway serving the National Capital Region alongside Delhi's existing Indira Gandhi International Airport, and it has been positioned as a future cargo and passenger hub for western Uttar Pradesh. The Cabinet's own framing, that it will become the state's largest airport and potentially the country's largest aviation hub, signals the scale of ambition, though that status depends on construction and traffic ramping up over years, not on the rename itself.

This comes in a week when Indian aviation also saw the Smit Machchhar Flydubai story continue (he is set to receive an Israeli civilian award for his role in averting a cockpit hijacking), and when Gulf carriers were suspending Riyadh flights over the Houthi attack. Jewar's renaming is a domestic, largely symbolic story by comparison, but it is still relevant to anyone tracking India's airport capacity build-out, since Jewar is one of the country's most closely watched new-airport projects.

Watch for the commissioning timeline for the airport itself, any further announcements on cargo and airline commitments, and whether the renaming requires separate central government sign-off beyond the state Cabinet's approval.

facts.fact: Jewar airport approved for renaming to Narendra Modi International Airport, Noida-Jewar, by UP Cabinet

articles.title: OpenAI's annualised revenue nears $50 billion, below some recent reports, as it races Anthropic
articles.summary: OpenAI is on track for about $50 billion in annualised revenue, an increase from last year but below a recently reported $70 billion figure. The gap stems partly from how OpenAI and Anthropic each count cloud-provider sales.
articles.body:
OpenAI is on track to generate annualised revenue of roughly $50 billion based on its current performance, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. That is an increase from the prior year, but it is below some recently reported estimates for the company. Some outlets reported last month that OpenAI was already on track for nearly $70 billion in annualised revenue; the Financial Times, which first reported the revised, lower estimate, said the discrepancy comes from attempts by OpenAI's own investors to compare its figures more directly with rival Anthropic, including how each company accounts for sales made through cloud providers. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on the figure.

Annualised revenue, a projection of yearly sales based on a shorter recent period, has become a headline metric that both OpenAI and Anthropic tout as evidence of growth, but the companies do not measure it the same way, which is exactly what is creating the gap in outside reporting. Bloomberg News had previously reported that Anthropic's annualised revenue hit $65 billion by the end of July, putting Anthropic ahead of OpenAI on that specific metric as the two companies compete intensely to sign up business customers.

Both firms have filed confidential paperwork to go public, with Anthropic expected to list as soon as this fall. OpenAI, by contrast, has said it no longer expects to IPO this year, as it focuses on addressing safety concerns about its technology, a point that connects to this week's separate reporting on fired OpenAI safety researchers and on Anthropic's own IPO prospectus warning about AI's catastrophic risks. OpenAI is currently in discussions with investors to raise $30 billion or more in a funding round that would value the company at about $1.4 trillion.

The trajectory is still upward. OpenAI was previously reported to be on pace for more than $40 billion in annualised revenue as of August, so the move to roughly $50 billion reflects real acceleration, driven by businesses adopting its newer models and coding tools, even if the number is lower than the most optimistic reports suggested.

For anyone valuing either company ahead of an IPO, the lesson is that annualised revenue claims from AI labs need to be read carefully: the same underlying business can be described very differently depending on what counts as revenue. Watch for OpenAI's own disclosures if and when it moves toward a public listing, and for Anthropic's IPO prospectus details as its listing approaches.

articles.title: Anthropic launches Claude Haiku 5.5, its third new model in a month, ahead of planned IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5, priced 75% below its predecessor and aimed at tasks like classification and live support. It is the company's first Haiku model with built-in safeguards for high-risk cybersecurity requests.
articles.body:
Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on Wednesday, the third model in its Claude 5.5 family released within the past month, as the company continues to expand its AI lineup ahead of a planned IPO. Haiku 5.5 is built for lighter, high-volume tasks such as classification, summarisation and extraction, including live customer support, voice agents and in-app assistants, rather than the complex reasoning work aimed at Anthropic's larger models.

The pricing change is the headline detail: Haiku 5.5 costs 75% less than its predecessor, Haiku 4.5. For prompts under 100,000 tokens, it is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, rising to $0.50 and $2.50 respectively for longer prompts. That is a significant cost reduction for the kind of high-volume, repetitive tasks Haiku-class models are built to handle, and it continues a broader industry pattern of smaller models getting cheaper even as flagship models push the frontier on capability.

Anthropic also said this is its first Haiku model with built-in safeguards for a narrow set of high-risk cybersecurity requests, while stating that most everyday tasks will not be affected by those safeguards. That detail is notable given the company's public positioning this week: Anthropic's own IPO prospectus, reported separately, has warned that advanced AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks, and the company's leadership has been vocal about slowing the pace of AI development industry-wide even as it keeps shipping new models at a rapid clip.

The release lands in a week of intense competitive activity between Anthropic and OpenAI, both racing toward IPOs and both disclosing revenue figures that are being parsed closely by investors. Three Claude 5.5 models in a month is an aggressive release cadence for a company that is simultaneously preparing public-market disclosures, and it signals that Anthropic wants its product pipeline, not just its safety messaging, in front of investors as the IPO approaches.

For businesses evaluating AI vendors, the price cut on Haiku-class work is the practical takeaway: tasks like support-ticket classification or document extraction, which are high-volume and cost-sensitive, just got cheaper to run on Claude. Watch for Anthropic's next model release and for any further detail on the IPO timeline.

articles.title: GST Council scraps officers' arrest powers, eases refunds for small businesses, leaves rates unchanged
articles.summary: India's GST Council left tax rates unchanged at its 57th meeting but removed officers' power to arrest taxpayers, raised the prosecution threshold fivefold, and sped up refund processing. The reforms take effect from April 2027.
articles.body:
The GST Council, at its 57th meeting on Thursday, approved a set of compliance and enforcement reforms while leaving tax rates unchanged. The most significant change is the removal of GST officers' power to arrest individuals under the GST law. The Council also raised the monetary threshold for initiating prosecution fivefold, from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore, and removed the provision for minimum punishment, leaving decisions on fines or imprisonment entirely to judicial discretion. The general penalty, which applies where no specific penalty is prescribed, was cut from Rs 25,000 to Rs 10,000.

Refund processing gets faster under the new rules. The time limit for acknowledging a refund claim drops from 15 days to 10, and a claim is now deemed acknowledged automatically if no acknowledgement or deficiency notice is issued within that window. Ninety percent of eligible refund claims will be sanctioned automatically after a risk assessment, with orders issued within three working days instead of seven. Refunds of excess balances sitting in electronic cash ledgers become fully automatic.

Small businesses and e-commerce sellers get specific relief. The Council approved, in principle, an optional annual-return scheme for businesses with turnover up to Rs 5 crore that supply exclusively to consumers: eligible taxpayers can file returns annually while still paying GST quarterly, cutting the compliance burden for genuinely small operators. The Council also simplified registration for small sellers on e-commerce platforms.

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said these reforms will be implemented from April 1, 2027, the start of the next financial year, giving businesses and tax administration more than a year to prepare. The Council also decided that GST rate-related matters will now be taken up only once a year, at a meeting dedicated exclusively to tax rates, separating the rate-setting process from the ongoing compliance and enforcement agenda.

Taken together, the reforms shift GST enforcement away from coercive powers like arrest and toward faster, more automated processing, while keeping the headline tax-rate question off the table for this cycle. For small businesses and exporters, the faster refund timelines and simplified registration are the parts most likely to be felt directly; for larger taxpayers, the removal of arrest powers and the higher prosecution threshold reduce one source of compliance risk, even as ordinary tax recovery, interest and penalties for late filing or errors remain unchanged.

categories: Economy & Banking bodies (RBI, SEBI, NABARD, IBRD, IMF, etc.)

facts.fact: GST prosecution threshold raised from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore

articles.title: World Bank raises India's FY27 growth forecast to 7.1%, warns on AI adoption gap and ageing workforce
articles.summary: The World Bank raised its India growth forecast ahead of the RBI's own policy decision, citing strength outside agriculture. It also warned that South Asia's demographic advantage is fading and that AI adoption in Indian firms lags the US.
articles.body:
The World Bank raised its growth forecast for India in FY27 (2026-27), citing strength in the rest of the economy offsetting weakness from sub-par monsoons, which the bank expects to reduce agricultural output and rural demand while pushing up food inflation on top of already elevated energy prices. For FY28 (2027-28), the World Bank expects Indian growth of 7.2%. The revision landed a day before the RBI's own interest-rate decision, with economists widely expecting a 25-basis-point hike, and the RBI's own statement went on to raise its FY27 growth forecast by 40 basis points to 7.1%, matching the World Bank's upgraded number.

The upward revisions have been a pattern across forecasters this cycle. India's growth has exceeded expectations for some time, helped by a rapid April-June quarter growth rate of 7.8%. On September 23, four international agencies, S&P Global Ratings, Fitch Ratings, the OECD and the Asian Development Bank, all raised their growth forecasts for the current fiscal year by 40 to 80 basis points, to a range of 6.9% to 7.1%.

The World Bank's report, titled 'Adopting AI for Growth', paired the growth upgrade with two structural warnings. First, on demographics: South Asia's working-age population growth is projected to drop from 2.2% a year between 1960 and 2023 to just 0.6% a year over the next 25 years, and the bank described the region's transition to an "aged" population structure as unusually compressed relative to the income levels at which other emerging economies made the same transition. Its recommended response is to address labour-market and ageing policy simultaneously rather than sequentially.

Second, on AI adoption: only 23% of Indian firms report using AI, compared with 43% in the US, though that headline comparison does not account for differences in the type of AI technology used or how deeply it is embedded in business operations. On the World Bank's own AI Adoption Index, which weighs factors like software purchases, use of advanced AI technologies and the number of core business functions using AI, India scores 0.27 against the US's 0.85. More worryingly for the growth story, the bank found that expected AI gains are concentrated in a small number of Indian firms: almost 75% of firms expect little to no productivity benefit from AI at all, and 15% actually expect faster AI development to reduce their revenue per worker by up to 10%, likely because they expect to lose market share to better-positioned competitors.

For India's growth outlook, the message is two-sided: near-term momentum is strong enough that forecasters keep revising growth up, but the World Bank's own report flags that the AI transition most of the world is betting on could widen gaps between Indian firms rather than lift all of them, at the same time as the demographic dividend that has underpinned India's growth story for decades is starting to fade.

briefs.text: Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar will receive Israel's Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism for his role in averting a hijacking after his co-pilot allegedly attacked him in the cockpit. Reports say he kept the crew able to overpower the attacker despite his injuries.
An RBI survey found household inflation expectations for the next year have hit 10%. The reading adds context to the central bank's decision to shift its policy stance toward tightening.
An RBI survey found rural consumer confidence has worsened for six consecutive months. The trend points to pressure on rural demand even as headline GDP forecasts are being revised upward.
New UPI charges apply for payments above Rs 5,000 made after October 15, according to RBI guidance. The change affects a narrow band of larger digital payments, not routine small transactions.

An IndiGo aircraft was damaged by a lightning strike and made a safe landing in Lucknow. No injuries were reported, and the incident is a reminder of weather-related operational risk even on routine domestic routes.
IndiGo raised its fuel charge, which is likely to push airfares higher, as fuel prices rise following the West Asia conflict. The increase will feed through to ticket prices on domestic routes.
SEBI urged retail investors not to blindly follow stock tips and to understand an investment before making it. The advisory comes amid continued retail participation in a volatile market.
Honeywell will accelerate engine deliveries to Hindustan Aeronautics Limited for trainer aircraft. Faster deliveries would help HAL's production timelines for India's military trainer programme.
Bharti Airtel's Sunil Mittal said he is looking forward to a successful listing for rival Reliance Jio. The comment is notable coming from a direct competitor in India's telecom market.

An explainer examines why Elon Musk's Starlink is in conflict with India's established telecom operators. The dispute centres on how satellite broadband should be licensed and priced against terrestrial networks.

Google Cloud introduced a Gemini-based agent aimed at workplace tasks, as the AI agent race among big tech firms intensifies. It follows a wave of enterprise agent launches from rivals including OpenAI and Anthropic.

OpenAI said it disrupted influence operations linked to Iran and Russia that were using its tools. The disclosure is part of OpenAI's periodic reporting on misuse of its models for state-linked campaigns.

Security researchers who say they were fired by OpenAI have accused the company of having a chilling effect on internal safety work. The allegation adds to a string of safety-related controversies at the company this month.
SoftBank is seeking $100 billion from Gulf investors to expand its AI investment bet. The fundraising push follows SoftBank's completed $30 billion investment in OpenAI reported earlier this week.
The US announced an effort to disrupt hacking infrastructure run by China's Integrity Tech Group. The action is part of ongoing US-China tension over state-linked cyber activity.

South Korea and Japan have faced a wave of hacks as AI tools lower the technical bar for cybercriminals. The trend mirrors warnings from security researchers about AI-assisted attacks becoming more accessible.
AMD chief executive Lisa Su is courting Korean AI chipmakers as the company competes with Nvidia for AI chip supply-chain partnerships. The move reflects intensifying competition in AI hardware.
ASML and Zeiss said next-generation chipmaking technology may be ready within a decade. The timeline matters for how far Moore's-law-style scaling can continue for AI chips.
Billionaire investor Ray Dalio said markets may be nearing a point where an AI bubble could burst. The warning adds a prominent voice to a growing debate over AI-driven valuations.
IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the time has come for AI regulation in India, and the government will release a consultation paper. It signals New Delhi moving toward a formal AI policy framework.
The RBI removed Paytm Payments Bank from its list of scheduled banks. The move is a further regulatory step following the RBI's earlier restrictions on the entity.

Hurricane Isaias has forced the shutdown of 63% of Gulf of Mexico oil output as Florida and Alabama brace for landfall. The disruption adds a fresh supply risk on top of existing West Asia-driven crude volatility.

Attacks in the Black Sea have disrupted yellow pea and sunflower oil supplies to India. The disruption affects Indian food-import costs at a time when the RBI is already watching food inflation closely.

RBI's sell-buy dollar swaps have slowed the rupee's fall but pushed up forward premiums, making it costlier for companies to hedge currency risk. The trade-off shows the cost of the central bank's currency defence.

The government is likely to finalise a critical-minerals stockpiling policy within a month. The policy would build strategic reserves of minerals needed for electronics, EVs and defence manufacturing.
Copper is set for a weekly gain as Chinese demand returns and supply concerns persist. The move tracks a broader pattern of industrial metals reacting to Chinese activity data.

IT stocks gained roughly Rs 70,000 crore in a single day despite the Trump administration's PERM suspension, as investors read the move as a long-run green-card issue rather than a near-term earnings threat. The reaction suggests markets are focused on Q2 results over immigration headlines for now.

Australia's Maas Group shares plunged 11% after Nvidia-backed Firmus scrapped its planned $5 billion IPO. The cancelled listing is a sign of selective caution returning to AI-infrastructure fundraising.

Palm oil producing countries are seeking closer ties with India, the world's largest vegetable oil importer. Deeper supply relationships would matter for India's edible-oil import costs and food inflation.
Regional airline FLY91 is scaling up its hiring as it expands operations. The push is a concrete data point for job-seekers tracking growth in India's regional aviation segment.

Industry leaders say India's semiconductor push and the rise of agentic AI are set to reshape telecom and connected devices. The comments tie India's chip manufacturing ambitions directly to the AI hardware cycle.

India's IT Secretary said the government wants a judicious mix of open and proprietary AI models to protect data. The statement signals New Delhi's approach to balancing AI capability with data-sovereignty concerns.
